title: Collaborative editor
summary: Real-time co-editing with OT or CRDTs, presence and history.
prompt: Design a collaborative document editor where several people edit the same document at once, see each other’s cursors, work offline briefly, and can view version history.

requirements: Functional: concurrent editing, live cursors and presence, comments, version history, offline edits that merge on reconnect.
Non-functional: local edits feel instant; remote edits appear within ~100s of ms; all replicas converge to the same document; edits are never lost.
estimation: Most documents have 1–5 concurrent editors; popular ones may have hundreds of viewers.
A fast typist produces ~10 operations/s; batching per 50–100 ms keeps message rates low.
Operation logs grow without bound, so snapshot periodically and compact old operations.
api: WebSocket per open document: client sends ops {baseRevision, ops}; server broadcasts accepted ops with the new revision.
GET /docs/{id}?revision= → snapshot plus ops after it; GET /docs/{id}/history for named versions.
data: Operation log per document: (doc_id, revision, author, ops, timestamp).
Snapshots every N revisions: (doc_id, revision, content).
Presence (cursors, selections) is ephemeral and kept only in memory.
design: Each document has one owning session server (routed by doc ID) that orders operations and persists them.
Clients apply edits locally at once and send them; the server transforms concurrent ops (OT) or merges them (CRDT), assigns revisions and broadcasts.
Offline clients queue ops and send them on reconnect with their base revision.
deepDives: Operational transformation: the server rewrites an op against concurrent ops it has already applied, so intent is kept (an insert after a deleted range shifts correctly). A central server keeps OT tractable.
CRDTs: each character gets a unique, ordered ID, so merges are commutative and need no central transform; the cost is metadata overhead and tombstones.
Version history: snapshots plus op ranges give any past version; named versions are pinned snapshots.
bottlenecks: A very popular document on one server: separate viewers (read-only broadcast fan-out) from editors.
Session server failure: clients reconnect; the new owner loads the latest snapshot and ops from the log.
Large documents: load and render incrementally; compact op logs.
tradeoffs: OT with a central server is efficient and well understood but needs that server; CRDTs support offline and peer-to-peer at a memory cost.
Persist every op for durability vs batch for throughput (risking a short window of loss).
Rich formatting and tables make transformation rules much more complex than plain text.

rubric.text: Applied edits optimistically on the client.
Resolved concurrent edits with OT or CRDTs and explained convergence.
Routed each document to an owner for ordering.
Persisted an operation log with periodic snapshots.
Compared OT and CRDT trade-offs with concrete costs.
Handled session server failover and hot documents.
